questions.stem: In which part of the testis are sperm produced?
options: The seminal vesicles
The seminiferous tubules
The epididymis
The vas deferens
questions.explanation: Sperm are made by meiosis in the walls of the coiled seminiferous tubules. They then pass to the epididymis, where they mature and are stored.

questions.stem: Why are the testes held in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity?
options: The testes need direct contact with the air to obtain oxygen
Sperm must be kept warmer than the rest of the body to survive
The abdomen has no room for organs that produce hormones
Sperm production works best a little below core temperature
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis is most effective slightly below core temperature, so the scrotum holds the testes outside the body cavity, and muscles move them closer or further to adjust temperature.

questions.stem: Which sequence traces the path of sperm from where they are made to where they leave the body?
options: Epididymis, seminiferous tubules, urethra, vas deferens
Seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ureter
Vas deferens, epididymis, seminiferous tubules, urethra
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra
questions.explanation: Sperm made in the seminiferous tubules mature in the epididymis, travel along the vas deferens during ejaculation, and leave through the urethra. The ureter carries urine from the kidney.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the fluid added by the seminal vesicles?
options: It carries testosterone to the female tract
It provides fructose as an energy source
It produces the sperm cells that are released
It stores sperm until the next ejaculation
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicle fluid is rich in fructose, which sperm use in respiration to power their tails, and it makes up a large part of semen's volume. Sperm are stored in the epididymis.

questions.stem: A man's vas deferens is blocked on both sides by scarring after an infection. What is the expected outcome?
options: He produces no semen at all, because all of its fluid comes from the testes
His sperm are released into the bladder and leave the body in urine
His semen contains no sperm, but his testosterone levels stay normal
His testes stop producing testosterone, but sperm still reach the semen
questions.explanation: Sperm cannot pass the blockage, so semen, mostly made by the glands further along, contains no sperm. Testosterone enters the blood directly from the testes, so hormone levels are unaffected.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells of the testes to produce testosterone?
options: Progesterone
Luteinising hormone (LH)
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Oxytocin
questions.explanation: LH from the anterior pituitary acts on interstitial cells to release testosterone. FSH acts on the cells of the seminiferous tubules to support sperm production.

questions.stem: A man takes high doses of synthetic testosterone. Why might his sperm production fall?
options: Testosterone directly destroys the developing sperm cells in the seminiferous tubules
Testosterone causes the vas deferens to close, so sperm are reabsorbed
High testosterone raises FSH so much that the testes are overstimulated
Negative feedback lowers GnRH, FSH and LH, so the testes are less stimulated
questions.explanation: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing FSH and LH. Without FSH stimulation and with less testosterone made inside the testes, sperm production falls.

questions.stem: Where does fertilisation normally take place?
options: In the lining of the uterus
Inside a follicle in the ovary
In the canal of the cervix
In the upper part of an oviduct
questions.explanation: The egg is swept into the oviduct after ovulation and fertilisation usually occurs in its upper part. The early embryo then moves to the uterus to implant.

questions.stem: How is the ovulated egg moved along the oviduct to the uterus?
options: By the flow of fluid from the ovary towards the uterus
By sperm pushing the egg as they swim towards it
By beating cilia and muscular contractions of the oviduct wall
By its own tail, which beats to propel it along the tube
questions.explanation: The egg cannot move by itself; fimbriae draw it into the tube and the cilia of the lining and peristalsis in the wall carry it along. Only sperm have tails.

questions.stem: What is the function of the endometrium?
options: It is the lining of the uterus in which an embryo implants
It is the muscle layer of the uterus that contracts in labour
It is the outer covering of the ovary that releases eggs
It is the passage connecting the uterus to the vagina
questions.explanation: The endometrium thickens and becomes rich in blood vessels and glands each cycle, ready for implantation; it is shed in menstruation if no pregnancy occurs. The muscular layer is the myometrium.

questions.stem: In a typical 28-day cycle, what causes ovulation at about day 14?
options: A surge of progesterone from the corpus luteum
A fall in follicle-stimulating hormone to zero
A surge of luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary
A sudden fall in oestrogen secreted by the developing follicle
questions.explanation: Rising oestrogen from the maturing follicle triggers a surge of LH (and FSH), which causes the follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte. Progesterone rises only after ovulation.

questions.stem: What forms from the follicle after ovulation, and what does it secrete?
options: The corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone
The endometrium, which secretes FSH and LH into the blood
The placenta, which secretes oxytocin and prolactin
A new primary follicle, which secretes testosterone
questions.explanation: The empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, whose progesterone maintains the thickened endometrium. If no pregnancy occurs, it degenerates after about two weeks.

questions.stem: Why does high oestrogen around mid-cycle cause an LH surge, when for most of the cycle oestrogen suppresses LH?
options: High oestrogen causes the ovary itself to begin secreting large amounts of LH
LH is released only when oestrogen has fallen to its lowest level in the cycle
Sustained high oestrogen switches to positive feedback on the pituitary
High oestrogen destroys the corpus luteum, which normally blocks LH release
questions.explanation: At low to moderate levels oestrogen exerts negative feedback, but a sustained high level from the mature follicle triggers positive feedback, producing the LH surge that causes ovulation.

questions.stem: If an egg is not fertilised, what sequence of events leads to menstruation?
options: The corpus luteum grows, progesterone rises and the endometrium is shed
FSH rises, the follicle ruptures and the endometrium thickens and bleeds
Oestrogen rises, LH surges and the endometrium is reabsorbed into the blood
The corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and the lining breaks down
questions.explanation: Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum breaks down; the fall in progesterone and oestrogen means the endometrium can no longer be maintained, so it is shed. Low hormone levels also allow FSH to rise and start a new cycle.

questions.stem: What is the main role of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in females?
options: Stimulating follicles to develop and secrete oestrogen
Maintaining the endometrium during the second half of the cycle
Causing the uterus to contract strongly during labour
Stimulating the mammary glands to produce milk after birth
questions.explanation: FSH from the anterior pituitary promotes growth of ovarian follicles, which secrete oestrogen. Maintaining the endometrium is the job of progesterone.

questions.stem: Which phases of the menstrual (uterine) cycle occur at the same time as the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle?
options: Menstruation and the secretory phase
The proliferative and secretory phases
Menstruation and the proliferative phase
The secretory phase only
questions.explanation: While follicles develop (follicular phase), the uterus first sheds its lining and then rebuilds it under oestrogen (proliferative phase). The secretory phase matches the luteal phase, after ovulation.

questions.stem: If an embryo implants, how is the corpus luteum prevented from degenerating?
options: The pituitary stops releasing all hormones until after the birth
The endometrium secretes FSH, which keeps stimulating the follicle
The embryo secretes oxytocin, which stops menstruation from starting
Cells of the embryo secrete hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) from the developing embryo keeps the corpus luteum producing progesterone until the placenta takes over. Pregnancy tests detect hCG in urine.

questions.stem: How many functional gametes are produced from one primary spermatocyte and from one primary oocyte?
options: Four sperm; one ovum
One sperm; four ova
Two sperm; two ova
Four sperm; four ova
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis gives four sperm per primary spermatocyte. In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally, giving one large ovum and small polar bodies that degenerate.

questions.stem: Why does oogenesis divide the cytoplasm unequally, forming polar bodies?
options: So the extra chromosomes from crossing over can be discarded in the polar bodies
So one cell keeps most of the cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo
So the polar bodies can be fertilised as well, producing identical twins
So the ovum has half as many chromosomes as the polar bodies produced with it
questions.explanation: Unequal division concentrates cytoplasm, organelles and food reserves in one large cell, which must sustain the embryo before implantation. Polar bodies carry the extra chromosome sets and degenerate.

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of meiosis in oogenesis is correct?
options: Oocytes form continuously from puberty, as sperm do in males
Primary oocytes form before birth; meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters
Primary oocytes form at puberty; meiosis II is completed before ovulation
Meiosis begins and ends within a single menstrual cycle in each oocyte
questions.explanation: Primary oocytes are formed in the foetus and arrested in prophase I. From puberty, one completes meiosis I each cycle, and the secondary oocyte released completes meiosis II only at fertilisation.

questions.stem: Which comparison of spermatogenesis and oogenesis is correct?
options: Both begin before birth and produce one gamete from each cell that enters meiosis
Both produce gametes continuously from birth until death at the same rate
Sperm are made throughout adult life; eggs are released only from puberty to menopause
Eggs are released throughout adult life; sperm production stops at about age fifty
questions.explanation: Sperm are produced continuously in huge numbers from puberty onwards. Eggs are released cyclically from a fixed store of oocytes between puberty and menopause.

questions.stem: An egg survives for about a day after ovulation, while sperm can survive in the female tract for up to about five days. When is intercourse most likely to result in conception?
options: Only during menstruation, when the endometrium is being shed
At any time in the cycle with equal probability
In the few days before ovulation and on the day of ovulation
Only in the week after ovulation, when progesterone is high
questions.explanation: Sperm already present when the egg is released can fertilise it, so the fertile window spans several days before ovulation plus about a day after. Soon after that the egg is no longer viable.

questions.stem: What is the role of the acrosome in a sperm cell?
options: It contains mitochondria that supply energy for the tail to move
It stores the sperm's haploid set of chromosomes
It produces fructose that the sperm uses as an energy source
It releases enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers
questions.explanation: The acrosome is a cap of enzymes on the head that allows the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida. Mitochondria are packed in the midpiece.

questions.stem: What happens in the week between fertilisation and implantation?
options: The zygote divides by meiosis to form a placenta in the oviduct
The zygote stays in the ovary until the endometrium is ready
The zygote forms all its organs before reaching the uterus
The zygote divides by mitosis to form a blastocyst
questions.explanation: Cleavage divisions by mitosis form a ball of cells, then a hollow blastocyst, which reaches the uterus and implants in the endometrium about a week after fertilisation.

questions.stem: Which germ layer gives rise to the nervous system and the outer layer of the skin?
options: Mesoderm
Endoderm
Chorion
Ectoderm
questions.explanation: The ectoderm forms the brain, spinal cord and nerves as well as the epidermis, hair and nails. The chorion is a membrane that helps form the placenta.

questions.stem: Which structures develop mainly from the mesoderm?
options: The liver, pancreas and the gut lining
Muscles, bones, the heart and blood
The brain, spinal cord and epidermis
The lining of the gut and the lungs
questions.explanation: The middle germ layer forms muscle, the skeleton, the circulatory system and blood, the kidneys and the reproductive organs. Linings of the gut and airways come from the endoderm.

questions.stem: Which structures develop mainly from the endoderm?
options: The linings of the gut and the airways
The skeleton and the skeletal muscles
The brain, spinal cord and nerves
The heart, blood vessels and blood
questions.explanation: The inner germ layer forms the epithelial lining of the gut and airways and organs that develop from the gut, such as the liver and pancreas.

questions.stem: From which tissues does the placenta form?
options: The mother's cervix and the embryo's mesoderm
The embryo's chorion and the mother's endometrium
The embryo's ectoderm and the mother's myometrium
The mother's ovary and the embryo's amnion
questions.explanation: Chorionic villi from the embryo grow into the endometrium, which supplies the maternal blood spaces. Together they form the placenta, joined to the foetus by the umbilical cord.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how materials are exchanged at the placenta?
options: The placenta stops all substances from the mother reaching the foetus
Substances cross between maternal and foetal blood, which do not mix
Maternal blood flows directly into the foetus through the umbilical vein
Foetal blood cells cross into the mother to collect oxygen from her lungs
questions.explanation: Maternal and foetal blood are separated by thin layers of tissue, across which oxygen, nutrients and antibodies pass to the foetus and carbon dioxide and urea pass to the mother. Some harmful substances also cross.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of labour, in order?
options: Dilation of the cervix, birth of the baby, delivery of the placenta
Birth of the baby, dilation of the cervix, delivery of the placenta
Delivery of the placenta, dilation of the cervix, birth of the baby
Dilation of the cervix, delivery of the placenta, birth of the baby
questions.explanation: Stage 1 dilates the cervix, stage 2 is the expulsion of the baby, and stage 3 is the delivery of the placenta and membranes, the afterbirth.

questions.stem: During labour, contractions push the baby against the cervix, which leads to more oxytocin release and stronger contractions. What type of control is this?
options: Positive feedback, which keeps the uterus relaxed until birth
Positive feedback, which amplifies the change until birth occurs
Negative feedback, which keeps contractions at a steady level
Negative feedback, which stops contractions once the cervix opens
questions.explanation: Stretch of the cervix triggers oxytocin release, causing stronger contractions and more stretch; the cycle intensifies until the baby is born. Negative feedback would reduce the contractions instead.

questions.stem: Before birth, the foramen ovale lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. Why is this useful in the foetus?
options: It mixes blood so the foetus gets equal amounts of oxygen in every vessel
It allows blood to reach the placenta without passing through the heart
It lets most blood bypass the lungs, which are not yet used to breathe
It lets blood bypass the liver, which is not yet working in the foetus
questions.explanation: The foetus gets oxygen from the placenta, so pumping all blood through the fluid-filled lungs would be wasteful. Bypassing the liver is the role of the ductus venosus.

questions.stem: At birth the baby's first breaths inflate the lungs. Which circulatory changes follow?
options: The umbilical arteries widen and carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the baby's heart
The ductus venosus opens so that blood bypasses the liver for the first few weeks after birth
The foramen ovale closes and the ductus arteriosus constricts, so blood flows to the lungs
The foramen ovale opens wider and the ductus arteriosus enlarges to carry more blood to the lungs
questions.explanation: Inflating the lungs lowers resistance in the pulmonary circuit; pressure in the left atrium then exceeds the right, closing the flap of the foramen ovale, and the ductus arteriosus constricts. The umbilical vessels close.

questions.stem: Which gland at the base of the brain releases FSH and LH?
options: The anterior pituitary
The thyroid gland
The adrenal gland
The pineal gland
questions.explanation: Under the control of GnRH from the hypothalamus, the anterior pituitary secretes FSH and LH in both sexes. The thyroid and adrenal glands produce other hormones.

questions.stem: Which hormone is mainly responsible for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty, such as a deeper voice and facial hair?
options: Testosterone
Oestrogen
Progesterone
Oxytocin
questions.explanation: Testosterone from the interstitial cells of the testes drives male secondary sexual characteristics and supports sperm production. Oestrogen has the corresponding role in females.

questions.stem: What is the role of the myometrium during birth?
options: It dilates to form the opening of the cervix
Its smooth muscle contracts to push the baby out
It thickens to provide nutrients for the baby
It produces hCG to maintain the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: The myometrium is the thick smooth muscle layer of the uterus; under oxytocin it contracts rhythmically in labour. The endometrium, not the myometrium, is the nutrient-rich lining.

questions.stem: Which part of a sperm cell contains many mitochondria, and why?
options: The tail tip, to digest the layers around the egg
The nucleus, to copy DNA before fertilisation
The midpiece, to supply ATP for the tail to beat
The head, to supply energy for the acrosome enzymes
questions.explanation: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria whose ATP powers the beating of the tail. The head carries the haploid nucleus and the acrosome.
